streams.title: Two-Eyed Seeing (Etuaptmumk)
streams.description: Bring the strengths of Indigenous ways of knowing and Western biological science into respectful dialogue, using both together to develop a fuller understanding of the topic.
streams.details: Consider what each knowledge system reveals, where their insights meet or differ, and how learning from both could inform action. Use Indigenous-authored or community-grounded sources wherever possible, keep knowledge connected to its people and place, and respect community protocols and restrictions.

streams.title: Toronto Zoo: comparative organismal biology
streams.description: Examine the topic by comparing at least three distinct plant and/or animal groups.
streams.details: Ask how differences and similarities in anatomy, physiology, behaviour, ecology, evolutionary history, or relationships with people shape the patterns you find. Toronto Zoo organisms and conservation programs may provide useful cases, but the topic does not have to be limited to zoo husbandry.

streams.title: Biological subdisciplines
streams.description: Examine the topic through at least three distinct biological subdisciplines.
streams.details: Possible subdisciplines include cell biology, molecular biology, genetics, genomics, physiology, development, behaviour, evolution, ecology, and conservation biology. Do more than present three separate summaries: show how the disciplines connect and what becomes clearer when their evidence is synthesized.

topics.title: Domestication and its biological limits
topics.description: Why have some species entered long-term relationships of domestication with people while others have not? Possible directions include behaviour, life history, genetics, ecology, cultural relationships, and the distinction between domestication, taming, and captive breeding.

topics.title: Microclimates and thermal stress
topics.description: Organisms experience temperature, humidity, wind, shade, and water at a local scale. How do microclimates affect biological performance and survival, and how can habitats—wild, urban, agricultural, or managed—support organisms facing unfamiliar or changing conditions?

topics.title: The gut–brain axis and protein misfolding
topics.description: Evidence suggests that misfolded proteins, microbes, inflammation, and neural signalling in the gut may contribute to neurodegenerative disease. How can research across organisms and biological scales clarify the gut–brain connection and point toward prevention or treatment?

topics.title: Cell-in-cell interactions and cancer
topics.description: Some cells engulf living neighbouring cells, a phenomenon observed in cancers and in other biological contexts. What causes cell-in-cell interactions, what functions might they serve, and how could understanding them improve cancer biology, diagnosis, or treatment?

topics.title: Seed dormancy and germination
topics.description: Seeds use diverse cues to remain dormant or begin germination. How do environmental conditions, physiology, evolutionary history, and relationships with people shape dormancy and the success of germination, cultivation, restoration, or seed banking?

topics.title: Mosquitoes as vectors for disease
topics.description: Mosquitoes can transmit viruses, parasites, and other pathogens, but only some species and populations are effective vectors. How do mosquito genetics, immunity, microbiomes, behaviour, host choice, climate, and habitat shape transmission, and how can that biology inform control?

topics.title: Seasonal indicators and ecological forecasting
topics.description: Flowering, leaf-out, insect emergence, migration, breeding, and other recurring events can signal seasonal change. How do organisms respond to environmental cues, how can observations be combined across places and scales, and what happens when interacting species respond at different rates?

topics.title: Antibiotic resistance
topics.description: An examination of how non-lethal concentrations of antibiotics influence the evolution of resistance in bacteria, could have implications for the development of resistance to new generation antibiotics. New discoveries show antibiotic resistance may predate the use of antibiotics.

topics.title: Circadian rhythms
topics.description: New research on how the circadian clock controls cellular processes could have implications for treatment of metabolic disorders. In addition, interesting work examines the adaptive significance of circadian clocks.

sources.label: National Institute of General Medical Sciences

topics.title: Proprioception and sensing body position
topics.description: Proprioception allows organisms to sense body position, movement, and force. How do proprioceptive systems differ across organisms, how are sensory signals integrated with movement, and what can failures or adaptations reveal about nervous-system function?

topics.title: Obesogens
topics.description: An intriguing hypothesis suggests that exposure of humans to harmful chemicals from the environment, including some that are routinely sprayed on fruits and vegetables, may be a factor in the obesity epidemic. Exploring how these chemicals impact our gut ecology could lead to a better understanding of how chronic illnesses associated with obesity may be triggered by changes in the gut microbiome.

topics.title: Mercury in biological systems
topics.description: Mercury moves through water, soil, food webs, and bodies. What determines its uptake, chemical transformation, biomagnification, and biological effects, and what approaches can improve monitoring, remediation, and ecosystem recovery?

topics.title: Regeneration and tissue engineering
topics.description: Living systems vary greatly in their capacity to repair or regenerate tissues. How can biological knowledge of cells, extracellular matrices, development, and naturally regenerating organisms inform tissue engineering, transplantation, and drug testing?

topics.title: High-altitude adaptation
topics.description: High altitude presents organisms with low oxygen, cold, intense radiation, and short growing seasons. How do organisms—including high-altitude human populations—acclimatize or adapt through physiology, behaviour, development, ecology, and evolution?

topics.title: The limits of biological performance
topics.description: Speed, endurance, strength, and recovery are constrained by trade-offs in anatomy, physiology, energy use, behaviour, and environment. What sets the limits of performance, and why do different organisms solve these challenges in different ways?

topics.title: Longevity and lifespan variation
topics.description: Lifespans vary from days to centuries. How do genetics, physiology, life history, ecology, behaviour, and environment interact to shape aging and longevity, and what can unusually long- or short-lived organisms teach us?

topics.title: Hibernation and metabolic suppression
topics.description: Many organisms survive difficult periods by suppressing metabolism, changing body temperature, or entering dormancy. How are these states controlled, what trade-offs do they create, and could understanding them inform conservation, medicine, or human space travel?

topics.title: The origins of life on Earth
topics.description: There is perhaps no more fundamental question in biology than that of the origins of life. One hypothesis proposes that life arose in hydrothermal vents, openings in the ocean floor from which hot, alkaline, mineral-rich water emerges. Interestingly, hydrothermal vents and the unique, often endemic life that inhabit them, were not even discovered until the 1970s.

topics.title: Astrobiology: life beyond Earth
topics.description: While no definitive evidence of extraterrestrial life has been found, research in astrobiology is fueled by discoveries like the potential for liquid water on other planets and the existence of extremophiles, organisms that thrive in harsh conditions on Earth.

topics.title: Biological effects of road salt
topics.description: Winter road salt moves into soils, plants, groundwater, rivers, and lakes. How does increasing salinity affect organisms and ecological relationships, which biological traits predict vulnerability or tolerance, and what alternatives or mitigation strategies are possible?

topics.title: The biological challenge of salt and water balance
topics.description: All organisms must balance water and dissolved ions, but freshwater, marine, terrestrial, and drought-prone environments create very different challenges. How do organisms obtain water, regulate salts, and cope when environmental salinity changes?

topics.title: Thermoregulation in extinct and living animals
topics.description: Animals occupy a continuum of strategies for producing, retaining, and exchanging heat. How can evidence from living organisms, fossils, anatomy, chemistry, behaviour, and environments be combined to infer thermoregulation in extinct animals such as dinosaurs?

topics.title: Biological limits of heat tolerance
topics.description: Extreme heat challenges cellular function, water balance, behaviour, reproduction, and survival. What sets heat limits across organisms, how do acclimatization and adaptation alter those limits, and how might biological and community knowledge guide responses to a warming climate?

topics.title: Sleep across animals
topics.description: Sleep-like states occur in organisms with very different nervous systems and lifestyles. What functions does sleep serve, how is it regulated, and what can variation across organisms reveal about its evolution and biological importance?

topics.title: Freeze tolerance and survival below 0°C
topics.description: Freezing threatens cells and tissues, yet some plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms survive it. What molecular, physiological, behavioural, and ecological strategies prevent damage or permit recovery after freezing?

topics.title: Animal migration
topics.description: There are many notable examples of animal migrations. Bar-tailed godwits fly over 11,000km from Alaska to New Zealand over 8 days without stopping; wildebeests migrate on a loop through Kenya and Tanzania following the seasonal rains but experiencing massive deaths; and monarchs migrate from Canada to Mexico, a journey which was revealed by the help of citizen-scientists. The reasons for these migrations are often mysterious, and, in response to climate change, some species are no longer migrating.

topics.title: White-nose syndrome and emerging wildlife disease
topics.description: White-nose syndrome shows how a pathogen, host biology, environmental conditions, and ecological relationships can combine to cause wildlife declines with consequences beyond the affected species. What controls susceptibility, spread, ecosystem effects, and the success of intervention?

topics.title: Dietary antioxidants
topics.description: The mitochondrial oxidative stress theory of aging posits that aging is the result of an accumulation of oxidative damage to protein, membranes, and DNA caused by mitochondrially-derived reactive oxygen species (ROS). On this basis, the consumption of dietary antioxidants has been proposed as a method to extend lifespan, hence so many foods are enriched with antioxidants (or their natural antioxidant content is highlighted). However, some contend that the consumption of antioxidants is merely hype.

sources.label: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health

topics.title: Bioluminescence across living systems
topics.description: Organisms from bacteria and fungi to insects and deep-sea animals produce light. How does bioluminescence work, what functions does it serve, how has it evolved, and how have people applied or interpreted this biological phenomenon?

topics.title: Pathogen virulence: “Live fast and die young, or go slow and steady?”
topics.description: Some pathogens are highly damaging to their hosts, spreading very quickly but also killing almost everyone they infect (e.g. Ebola). Others are equally lethal, but may go without symptoms for years (e.g. HIV/AIDS). Yet others are more benign, and may only mildly or temporarily damage their hosts, only killing ones that are already weak (e.g. the Flu). From a parasite's (evolutionary) perspective, there seem to be pros and cons to all strategies: A parasite essentially uses hosts as a resource to ensure it completes its life cycle and spreads its offspring. But if it causes too much damage and kills the host too quickly, it may not get a chance to do so.

topics.title: Host-manipulating parasites and parasitoids
topics.description: Parasites and parasitoids can be master manipulators. Some can make rats walk up to cats, while others can make grasshoppers drown themselves. Some fungi can make ants climb up plants to position themselves just at the right height, temperature and humidity for the fungus to grow. The list is long, reads like science fiction, and makes one wonder to what degree parasites may be puppet masters driving population and ecosystem dynamics.

topics.title: The landscape of fear
topics.description: Animals often trade access to food, mates, or shelter against the risk of encountering predators. How do these perceived risks shape movement, physiology, behaviour, species interactions, and ecosystem processes, and how can ecologists map or test a landscape of fear?

topics.title: Forest management and fire
topics.description: For millions of years, ecosystems have relied on fire to replenish soils and stimulate plant growth, a practice historically managed through controlled, low-intensity burning by various groups. How does the biodiversity and resilience of forests maintained by controlled burns compare to forests shaped by decades of modern systemic fire suppression?

topics.title: The impact of wildfires on animals and plants
topics.description: As wildfires force mass evacuations and destroy homes and businesses, one cannot help but wonder what effect wildfires have on the animals and plants inhabiting those same regions. Do they evacuate? Do they die? And what happens to the flora and fauna of a region in the aftermath of a wildfire?

topics.title: Energy balance in changing environments
topics.description: Environmental change can disrupt when, where, and how organisms acquire and spend energy. How do anatomy, physiology, behaviour, food webs, and seasonal timing shape energy balance and vulnerability? Polar bears and declining sea ice provide one important case study.

topics.title: Allee effects and the benefits of group living
topics.description: In many organisms, individual survival or reproduction declines when a population becomes too small or sparse. What biological mechanisms create Allee effects, how do they differ among living systems, and how should they influence conservation, restoration, or management?

topics.title: The theory of autumn colours
topics.description: At some point in your life, you have probably learned that the brilliant autumn displays of color are simply a byproduct of chlorophyll breaking down in preparation for the winter. An alternative, or complementary, hypothesis is that autumn colors function as an active and honest signal of a tree's defensive abilities against parasites. Trees invest in being colorful.

topics.title: Transmissible cancers and disease evolution
topics.description: Rare cancers can pass between individuals as living cell lineages. What makes transmission and immune escape possible, how do hosts and tumours coevolve, and what are the consequences for populations? Compare cases in dogs, Tasmanian devils, bivalves, and the recently documented transmissible melanoma of brown bullhead catfish.

topics.title: Climate change and the shifting geography of disease
topics.description: Changing temperature, rainfall, seasonality, and extreme weather can alter the ranges and timing of hosts, vectors, and pathogens. How might these changes reshape diseases such as malaria, dengue, Lyme disease, or wildlife infections, and why do land use, behaviour, surveillance, and health systems also matter?

sources.label: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences

topics.title: Noise pollution and biological communication
topics.description: Many organisms use sound to navigate, find food or mates, avoid danger, and communicate. How does human-made noise alter sensory systems, behaviour, physiology, ecological relationships, and survival in aquatic or terrestrial environments?

topics.title: Controlling insect populations
topics.description: Some insects may be pests, damaging agricultural crops, for example, or transmitting diseases. The importance of controlling such pests has led researchers to try multiple chemical and biological strategies: spraying insecticides, attracting insects into traps using pheromones, or introducing natural predators or diseases of the pest are only a few of them. Combining multiple approaches is often the best strategy, but there is no single recipe that fits all scenarios.

topics.title: Microplastics in biological systems
topics.description: Microplastics—plastic particles smaller than 5 mm—are found in water, soil, air, food webs, and bodies. How do their size, chemistry, movement, uptake, and biological effects vary among organisms and environments?

topics.title: Tracking animal movement
topics.description: GPS tags, radio telemetry, accelerometers, camera traps, acoustic arrays, stable isotopes, and community observations can reveal where and how animals move. What can different methods measure across species and scales, what biases or welfare costs do they introduce, and how should movement data guide conservation?

topics.title: Navigation and disrupted migration
topics.description: Migratory organisms navigate across unfamiliar landscapes using diverse sensory cues and inherited or learned information. How does navigation work, and how do habitat change, climate, pollution, or other disturbances affect migration? Monarch butterflies provide one possible case study.

topics.title: Camouflage, mimicry, and biological deception
topics.description: Organisms can avoid detection, imitate other species, or manipulate how receivers interpret signals. How do genetics, development, sensory systems, behaviour, ecology, and evolution produce camouflage and mimicry, and how do predators, prey, pollinators, or hosts respond?

sources.label: Animal camouflage: current issues and new perspectives
Signals, cues and the nature of mimicry

topics.title: Tool use in animals
topics.description: From hammers to saws, knives to fishing poles, and backhoes to dump trucks, humans have developed several tools to aid their daily chores. But are humans the only animals that utilize tools? And does tool use reflect a species' intelligence?

topics.title: Medicinal plants and biological activity
topics.description: Plants produce diverse compounds that can affect cells, microbes, parasites, and whole organisms. How do plant chemistry, physiology, ecology, cultivation, dose, and preparation shape biological activity, and how can promising effects be tested safely and responsibly?

topics.title: Environment-dependent sex determination
topics.description: Sex determination in humans is chromosome-based: XX zygotes will develop into females, and XY zygotes will develop into males. (Notwithstanding, the Internet is full of webpages describing how to conceive a boy or a girl.) There are some species, however, where sex determination is based on some aspect of the environment, such as temperature and species density. What are the advantages and disadvantages of such a system for sex determination, esp. in the face of a warming planet?

topics.title: The evolution and biology of parental care
topics.description: Parental care ranges from none to prolonged and cooperative investment, and occurs in many animal groups. What ecological, physiological, developmental, behavioural, and evolutionary factors favour different forms of care?

topics.title: Insects as sustainable food sources
topics.description: While the majority of North Americans meet their demands for protein by consuming beef, pork, and chicken, a comprehensive analysis published in Science suggested that avoiding meat is the single biggest way to reduce your environmental impact on the planet. Edible insects show great potential as an environmentally friendly choice for food, but they can possibly feed a global population, estimated to reach 9 billion by 2050?

topics.title: Renewable energy and wildlife
topics.description: Renewable-energy infrastructure can affect organisms through collision, habitat change, noise, altered movement, or new ecological opportunities. How can knowledge of organismal biology, landscapes, and human priorities guide the design and placement of wind-energy systems?

topics.title: Environmental enrichment and behavioural welfare
topics.description: Animals in human care may lack opportunities, choices, or challenges found in other environments. How can evidence about sensory systems, cognition, behaviour, ecology, and individual needs guide enrichment and the assessment of welfare across species and settings?

topics.title: Ecosystem impacts of nuclear radiation
topics.description: There have been several large-scale nuclear power plant accidents since the 1960s (e.g., Chernobyl, Fukushima). How do these accidents impact the flora and fauna surrounding the plant and beyond?

topics.title: Ecosystem impacts of oil spills
topics.description: There are several long-distance oil pipelines that traverse across Canada, and, according to records maintained by the The National Energy Board since the mid-20th century, millions of litres of oil have spilled from these pipelines at various locations, contaminating the environment. What are the impacts of oil spills on animals, plants, fungi, and micro-organisms? What role, if any, can living organisms play in terms of environmental remediation of oil spills?

sources.label: NOAA Office of Response and Restoration

topics.title: The role of artificial intelligence (AI) in biology
topics.description: While many undergraduate students have come to think of Al as "that thing my prof and TA told me I better not be using for my assignments", many scientists are curious about how Al might have a beneficial role to play in biological research, conservation, medicine, etc. Others are worried that Al may hamper scientific progress or unleash unpredictable disasters.

topics.title: Nutritional ecology and managed diets
topics.description: Diet involves nutrients, toxins, physical processing, foraging behaviour, microbes, seasonal availability, and cultural or management decisions. How can nutritional ecology guide diets for organisms in human care while accounting for species differences and natural feeding biology?

sources.label: Journal of Zoo and Aquarium Research

topics.title: Psychoactive substances and animal behaviour
topics.description: Animals encounter fermented foods, plant toxins, and other compounds that affect nervous-system function. Which claims about deliberate use are supported by evidence, how do effects vary across organisms, and what might this reveal about ecology, behaviour, reward, and addiction?

topics.title: Surviving mass extinctions
topics.description: While some controversy remains regarding whether or not we are currently experiencing the Earth's sixth mass extinction, there is no controversy that Earth has experienced five mass extinction events previously, the last one taking place about 65 million years ago and notoriously wiping out the dinosaurs. While between 75-95% of all species were lost in these mass extinction events, that also means that 5-25% of all species survived. Why are some species able to survive these mass extinction events? And do these species provide lessons for humanity as its own existence is threatened?

topics.title: Urban wildlife and rat population growth
topics.description: Cities create novel habitats, food sources, risks, and relationships among people and other organisms. Why do rats thrive in many urban environments, how might climate change alter their populations, and what can biology and community knowledge contribute to effective and ethical management?

topics.title: Zoonotic disease, One Health, and biosecurity
topics.description: Human, animal, plant, and ecosystem health are interconnected. What biological and social factors drive pathogen spillover among species, and how can surveillance, habitat stewardship, animal care, public health, and biosecurity reduce risk without ignoring local knowledge or ecological consequences?

quiz.title: Discover your Avengers teamwork style
quiz.intro: We’re going on a trip this weekend. Choose the option that feels most like you—even if none is perfect—and we’ll match you with an Avenger whose teamwork style resembles yours. There are no better or worse results.

traits.name: Coordination
traits.description: Creating structure, momentum, and shared accountability

traits.name: Analysis
traits.description: Examining evidence carefully and spotting important details

traits.name: Innovation
traits.description: Generating original ideas and making unexpected connections

traits.name: Connection
traits.description: Building trust, inclusion, and productive communication

traits.name: Adaptability
traits.description: Responding calmly and effectively when circumstances change

outcomes.name: Captain America
outcomes.description: You bring reliability, clear standards, and concern for the people affected by a decision.
outcomes.watchOut: Leave room for the plan to change when a teammate finds a better route.

outcomes.name: Spider-Man
outcomes.description: You learn quickly, make energetic connections, and want your work to help other people.
outcomes.watchOut: Choose priorities deliberately so enthusiasm does not become overcommitment.

outcomes.name: Iron Man
outcomes.description: You bring ambitious ideas, technical curiosity, and a willingness to test unconventional solutions.
outcomes.watchOut: Make sure the whole team understands and owns an idea before racing ahead.

outcomes.name: Scarlet Witch
outcomes.description: You bring imagination, emotional insight, and a strong sense of what matters beneath the surface.
outcomes.watchOut: Make your reasoning visible so teammates can act on insights that may feel intuitive to you.

outcomes.name: Hulk / Bruce Banner
outcomes.description: You dig beneath the surface, interrogate evidence, and help the group avoid conclusions the data cannot support.
outcomes.watchOut: Do not wait for perfect certainty before sharing a useful provisional conclusion.

outcomes.name: Hawkeye
outcomes.description: You bring preparation, practical judgment, and loyalty when a group needs dependable follow-through.
outcomes.watchOut: Invite unfamiliar possibilities before defaulting to the safest proven route.

outcomes.name: Ant-Man
outcomes.description: You bring spontaneity, humour, and a willingness to act when a group needs momentum.
outcomes.watchOut: Protect enough structure and focus to carry an exciting start through to completion.

outcomes.name: Captain Marvel
outcomes.description: You are comfortable taking responsibility and moving the group forward when the path is uncertain.
outcomes.watchOut: Invite quieter teammates into the decision before taking the lead.

outcomes.name: Vision
outcomes.description: You bring systems thinking, independence, and a calm focus on the long-term objective.
outcomes.watchOut: Check that an elegant strategy also reflects the team’s practical and interpersonal needs.

outcomes.name: Black Panther
outcomes.description: You combine long-range thinking, careful judgment, and respect for the perspectives around the table.
outcomes.watchOut: Translate strategy into early concrete actions so the group can build momentum.

questions.prompt: First, who are you going with?

options.label: A few close friends who already know one another well
Members of my family
People I do not know well yet—it could be a good way to connect
Whoever is excited and available at the last minute

questions.prompt: First, what kind of destination sounds best?

options.label: A walkable city with museums, neighbourhoods, and a carefully chosen home base
A quiet cabin where everyone can recharge and explore at their own pace
Somewhere none of us has visited—we will discover what makes it interesting
A lively festival or event with lots for the group to experience together

questions.prompt: The group chat asks who wants to organize. What do you do?

options.label: Build a shared itinerary with times, costs, and responsibilities
Research the best options and send everyone a concise comparison
Pitch one memorable idea that turns an ordinary trip into an adventure
Ask what everyone wants and help find the choice that includes them

questions.prompt: The group cannot agree on the main activity. How do you help?

options.label: Clarify the options and facilitate a quick, fair decision
Compare travel time, cost, reviews, and what each option actually offers
Invent a hybrid plan that captures the best part of two ideas
Read the room and suggest the compromise people will genuinely enjoy
A well-reviewed restaurant reserved ahead, with options for everyone
A local specialty I researched because food should teach us something about the place
A food market where everyone can choose something and we can share
Ingredients from a local shop, then we improvise a meal together

questions.prompt: You unexpectedly gain a free afternoon. What sounds best?

options.label: A museum, science centre, or guided tour with something new to learn
A hike, paddle, escape room, or other shared challenge
I can organize a compact itinerary so we make the most of it
Wander without a fixed route and see what hidden place we discover

questions.prompt: You are sharing accommodations with several people. You tend to…

options.label: Set a few expectations early so small issues never become big ones
Notice routines and quietly avoid making life harder for anyone
Stay flexible—different people need different things
Create the playlist, snacks, or game that makes the space feel shared

questions.prompt: By Sunday morning, the group is tired and losing momentum. You…

options.label: Narrow the plan to the two priorities that matter most
Figure out what is draining the group and solve that problem
Change the format completely; a fresh approach can reset the energy
Check in with everyone and rebuild the sense that we are doing this together

questions.prompt: Which contribution would you most naturally make to the trip?

options.label: Keeping the timeline and shared responsibilities from slipping
Finding the reliable information that prevents weak decisions
Finding the original angle that makes the experience memorable
Making sure everyone is heard and feels part of the group

questions.prompt: A surprising opportunity appears, but it would change the plan. What wins you over?

options.label: The evidence shows the benefits justify the risks
It is exactly the kind of unexpected experience we came for
We can revise the plan without abandoning our important commitments
The whole group lights up when we talk about doing it
